selectedEvidence.description2:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_
This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
selectedEvidence.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
selectedEvidence.profile: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.

mandatoryFoundation: ACCPPDE101 provides academic source searching, writing and reflective practice in the first term of both options.
comparability: The closest option has eight courses in art, archaeology and heritage, including Western painting analysis, Renaissance visual and architectural study, African art, ancient craft and Greek material culture, modern exhibitions and disciplinary history. History, film, literature, philosophy and qualitative research contribute concrete analytical or contextual skills. The degree comparison preserves dedicated gaps in long-run design and architecture, museums, aesthetics, excursion, preservation and thesis. For the alternate formal direction, six art and heritage courses provide art study, while six media courses and substantive work in communication and sociology support an emphasis on film, environmental images, media representation and publics. A separate architecture/design, heritage or museum option would not have sustained additional specialist teaching.

stoppingDecision.assessment: The historical option integrates the nine broad Art History interests through direct study of painting, objects, global art, museums and disciplinary methods, with narrower architectural and design coverage. The formal Arts, Media and Society direction supports a substantively different contemporary option. A standalone architecture/design or museum direction would require sustained specialist study beyond the available courses. The illustrative and career interests do not support further concepts.

repairs: The closest option replaces the performance-focused Creative Communication Laboratory with Philosophy of Emotion, a substantive philosophical complement to art interpretation. The second option retains the lab and starts Introductory Film & Media before Environmental Media, exchanging its term with the material media course. Correct GOSHIST312 to the current title and bound its claims to historical research.

Both ask how materials and making inform the interpretation of objects. UCR concentrates on ancient craft and archaeology, while Leiden treats techniques in art and architecture.
Both treat artistic traditions outside Europe and their interpretation across cultures. UCR focuses on African art, including collecting and repatriation.
